title: Reconcile first
hookLine: leave your gift at the altar and first be reconciled (Matthew 5:23–24)
tomorrow: why would anyone carry a stranger's load twice as far?

lines: A QUIET MINUTE, AND A NAME.
cards: Candle lit, song started, a quiet minute finally found, and a name drops in: a friend who got snapped at last week. That's yesterday's question. What do you do with it, right there?
Jesus answers with a scene, in the same sermon on the hill. Nobody in it is a villain. A man has brought his offering all the way to the altar.
The gift is in his hands. And in that moment, he remembers.

teach.b: "Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift."
Notice two things. The worship is already under way, and Jesus says stop: put the gift down, go. And notice who's upset.

Not "if you have something against him", but if your brother has something against you. The repair is yours to start. That's the teaching: in Christian life, peace with a person comes before the offering to God.
In the Catholic Mass, the sign of peace comes before communion, and some readers link it to this verse. Now the neighbor who shares it.
The Mishnah, a foundational collection of Jewish law, teaches that on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, wrongs between a person and God are atoned.
But wrongs between a person and another person are not atoned until he has made peace with the one he wronged. Same order: the person first. And an honest difference.

teach.h: A HOLY DAY THERE, ANY DAY HERE.
teach.b: In the Mishnah, this teaching sits inside a holy day each year and a whole practice of asking forgiveness.
In Matthew, it interrupts any offering on any day: leave it there, and go now. What the two share is a refusal of the shortcut: no settling things with God while a person is still waiting on you.

how: Christians read Matthew 5:23–24 as putting peace with others before worship; in the Catholic Mass the sign of peace comes before communion. In Jewish practice, people ask forgiveness of those they've wronged before Yom Kippur, following Mishnah Yoma 8:9.

o: forgiving someone only after they say sorry to you first
praying for an enemy instead of ever talking to them
putting repair with a person ahead of an offering to God

games.q: the gift and the repair: tap the pairs.
p: atones between a person and God

s: Jesus says finish your offering, then go and apologize
leave there thy gift before the altar, go first, then come back.
the Mishnah says Yom Kippur doesn't atone for wronging a person until you make peace
between a person and God, the day atones; between people, first make peace.
the verse is about when you're angry at someone else
it's when thy brother hath ought against thee: when they have something against you.

games.q: a coworker is still hurt by a joke you made, and you're about to lead a big presentation together. what would reconcile first do?
o: a short, honest word with them before the presentation, then do the work.
do the presentation first, and apologize only if they bring it up.
wait for them to come to you, since they're the one who's upset.
games.why: the gift waits at the altar while the man goes first. the work can wait a few minutes for the repair.

practice: Open your messages and find one person things are a little off with. Write one honest line of peace, no defense and no "but". Send it if it's ready; if it isn't, keep the version and sit quietly with their name.

wordCard.voice: Reconcile first: put the gift down, make peace with the one who has something against you, then come back and offer it.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 5:24: be reconciled, said as a command.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: reconcile first, and the gift will keep. Two days into the sermon.

sources.q: Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.

sources.ref: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 (Yom Kippur atones for wrongs between a person and God; not for wrongs between people until one appeases the other)
